claim: Phenotypic plasticity in eyespot size in response to environmental temperature observed in Bicyclus anynana satyrid butterflies is a complex derived adaptation of this lineage.
source: Here, we show that phenotypic plasticity in eyespot size in response to environmental temperature observed in Bicyclus anynana satyrid butterflies is a complex derived adaptation of this lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative phylogenetic analysis and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing the evolutionary origins of different components of the plastic response.

claim: 20E titer plasticity in response to temperature is a pre-adaptation shared by all butterfly species examined.
source: By reconstructing the evolution of known physiological and molecular components of eyespot size plasticity in a comparative framework, we showed that 20E titer plasticity in response to temperature is a pre-adaptation shared by all butterfly species examined
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of 20E titers across multiple species at different temperatures, showing consistent increases with temperature.

claim: Expression of EcR in eyespot centers is a derived trait found only in a subset of species with eyespots.
source: By reconstructing the evolution of known physiological and molecular components of eyespot size plasticity in a comparative framework, we showed that 20E titer plasticity in response to temperature is a pre-adaptation shared by all butterfly species examined, whereas expression of EcR in eyespot centers, and eyespot sensitivity to 20E, are both derived traits found only in a subset of species with eyespots.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing EcR expression patterns across different species and phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: Eyespot sensitivity to 20E is a derived trait found only in a subset of species with eyespots.
source: By reconstructing the evolution of known physiological and molecular components of eyespot size plasticity in a comparative framework, we showed that 20E titer plasticity in response to temperature is a pre-adaptation shared by all butterfly species examined, whereas expression of EcR in eyespot centers, and eyespot sensitivity to 20E, are both derived traits found only in a subset of species with eyespots.
evidence: This is supported by hormone injection experiments showing that only B. anynana eyespots respond to 20E manipulation at the wandering stage.

claim: Eyespot size plasticity in B. anynana is mostly controlled by temperature.
source: Eyespot size plasticity in B. anynana is mostly controlled by temperature, which leads to variable titers of the hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) at the wandering (Wr) stage of larval development (Monteiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and is consistent with the experimental data presented in the current study.

claim: Temperature leads to variable titers of the hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) at the wandering (Wr) stage of larval development in B. anynana.
source: Eyespot size plasticity in B. anynana is mostly controlled by temperature, which leads to variable titers of the hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) at the wandering (Wr) stage of larval development (Monteiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by hormone titer measurements in the current study.

claim: Manipulations of 20E signaling alone at the wandering stage are sufficient to modify eyespot size in B. anynana.
source: Manipulations of 20E signaling alone, at that time in development, are sufficient to modify eyespot size (Monteiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by the injection experiments in the current study.

claim: Central cells in B. anynana eyespots express the 20E receptor, Ecdysone Receptor (EcR).
source: This is because these central cells express the 20E receptor, Ecdysone Receptor (EcR), and upon sufficient 20E signaling, the active 20E-EcR complex is able to interact with yet unknown downstream genes to make these central cells divide and produce a larger central group of signaling cells (Bhardwaj et al., 2017) and ultimately a larger eyespot.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by immunostaining data in the current study.

claim: Upon sufficient 20E signaling, the active 20E-EcR complex is able to interact with yet unknown downstream genes to make central cells divide and produce a larger central group of signaling cells in B. anynana.
source: This is because these central cells express the 20E receptor, Ecdysone Receptor (EcR), and upon sufficient 20E signaling, the active 20E-EcR complex is able to interact with yet unknown downstream genes to make these central cells divide and produce a larger central group of signaling cells (Bhardwaj et al., 2017) and ultimately a larger eyespot.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work describing the mechanism.

claim: Eyespots originated once within the nymphalid family, about 85 mya.
source: Eyespots originated once within the nymphalid family, about 85 mya, likely from pre-existing simple spots of a single color (Oliver et al., 2012; Oliver et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: Eyespots likely originated from pre-existing simple spots of a single color.
source: Eyespots originated once within the nymphalid family, about 85 mya, likely from pre-existing simple spots of a single color (Oliver et al., 2012; Oliver et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: Five species showed no significant difference in hindwing (HW) Cu1 spot/eyespot size when reared across two temperatures and were deemed not plastic.
source: Five species showed no significant difference in hindwing (HW) Cu1 spot/eyespot size when reared across two temperatures and were deemed not plastic.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from rearing experiments at different temperatures.

claim: Most species showed a decrease in spot/eyespot size with an increase in temperature and had a negative slope in their reaction norms.
source: Most species showed a decrease in spot/eyespot size with an increase in temperature and had a negative slope in their reaction norms.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from rearing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: B. anynana was the only species which displayed a positive slope in its reaction norm, where eyespot size increased with temperature.
source: B. anynana was the only species which displayed a positive slope in its reaction norm, where eyespot size increased with temperature (Figure 1—source data—Table S2).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from rearing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ancestral character state reconstructions for the slope of reaction norms suggested that eyespot size plasticity of any form is a derived trait within nymphalids.
source: Ancestral character state reconstructions for the slope of these reaction norms suggested that eyespot size plasticity of any form is a derived trait within nymphalids, with three possible independent origins.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis using maximum parsimony methods.

claim: Eyespot size plasticity had three possible independent origins within nymphalids.
source: Ancestral character state reconstructions for the slope of these reaction norms suggested that eyespot size plasticity of any form is a derived trait within nymphalids, with three possible independent origins.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis using maximum parsimony methods.

claim: Ancestral species of nymphalids lacked plasticity in eyespot size.
source: Ancestral species of nymphalids lacked plasticity, whereas there were one or two independent origins of a negative response of eyespot size to increasing temperature and a separate origin of the opposing pattern of plasticity in ventral HW eyespot size in the Satyrid lineage, such as those leading to B. anynana (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There were one or two independent origins of a negative response of eyespot size to increasing temperature in nymphalids.
source: Ancestral species of nymphalids lacked plasticity, whereas there were one or two independent origins of a negative response of eyespot size to increasing temperature and a separate origin of the opposing pattern of plasticity in ventral HW eyespot size in the Satyrid lineage, such as those leading to B. anynana (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a separate origin of the opposing pattern of plasticity (positive response) in ventral HW eyespot size in the Satyrid lineage.
source: Ancestral species of nymphalids lacked plasticity, whereas there were one or two independent origins of a negative response of eyespot size to increasing temperature and a separate origin of the opposing pattern of plasticity in ventral HW eyespot size in the Satyrid lineage, such as those leading to B. anynana (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 20E titers at the wandering stage were consistently higher at the higher rearing temperature across all butterflies.
source: 20E titers at the wandering stage were consistently higher at the higher rearing temperature across all butterflies (Figure 2A) (Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by hormone titer measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EcR expression at the wandering stage was absent in species with no central wing spots (e.g., Danaus).
source: EcR expression at the wandering stage was absent in species with no central wing spots (e.g., Danaus), it was absent from spot centers in species with simple spots (e.g., Papilio and Idea), but was present in the eyespot central cells across all other species investigated, with a few exceptions (Junonia coenia (Koch et al., 2003) and Junonia almana) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EcR expression at the wandering stage was absent from spot centers in species with simple spots (e.g., Papilio and Idea).
source: EcR expression at the wandering stage was absent in species with no central wing spots (e.g., Danaus), it was absent from spot centers in species with simple spots (e.g., Papilio and Idea), but was present in the eyespot central cells across all other species investigated, with a few exceptions (Junonia coenia (Koch et al., 2003) and Junonia almana) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EcR expression at the wandering stage was present in the eyespot central cells across all other species investigated, with a few exceptions (Junonia coenia and Junonia almana).
source: EcR expression at the wandering stage was absent in species with no central wing spots (e.g., Danaus), it was absent from spot centers in species with simple spots (e.g., Papilio and Idea), but was present in the eyespot central cells across all other species investigated, with a few exceptions (Junonia coenia (Koch et al., 2003) and Junonia almana) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B and citation to previous work on J. coenia.

claim: Species with no EcR staining in spots still had EcR expression in the large polyploid nuclei that make up the peripodial membrane that wraps around each larval wing.
source: Species with no EcR staining in spots still had EcR expression in the large polyploid nuclei that make up the peripodial membrane that wraps around each larval wing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spot and eyespot focal marker gene Spalt was present in all species with eyespots or with simpler spots.
source: In contrast, the spot and eyespot focal marker gene Spalt, was present in all species with eyespots or with simpler spots, as previously reported (Oliver et al., 2012; Stoehr et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data and citations to previous work.

claim: The absence of EcR expression in J. coenia eyespots is restricted to the wandering stage of development.
source: The absence of EcR expression in J coenia eyespots is restricted to the wandering stage of development, as EcR is expressed in the eyespots of this species in later stages of development (Koch et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on J. coenia.

claim: EcR is expressed in the eyespots of J. coenia in later stages of development.
source: The absence of EcR expression in J coenia eyespots is restricted to the wandering stage of development, as EcR is expressed in the eyespots of this species in later stages of development (Koch et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on J. coenia.

claim: EcR localization in eyespots at the wandering stages of development is a derived trait, present only in species with eyespots.
source: The EcR expression data overall suggests that EcR localization in eyespots, at the wandering stages of development, is a derived trait, present only in species with eyespots.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative immunostaining data across species.

claim: Some eyespotted species subsequently lost EcR expression at the wandering stage of development.
source: Some of these eyespotted species subsequently lost EcR expression at this stage of development, a phenomenon previously reported for forewing Cu1 ventral eyespots in B. anynana females (Monteiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Idea leuconoe showed no response to 20E or EcR antagonist injections at the wandering stage.
source: Injections of 20E into female wanderers reared at low temperature (and with lower 20E titers) and of an EcR antagonist, CucB, into female wanderers reared at high temperature (and with higher 20E titers), showed no response across the first three species
evidence: This is supported by the injection experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Vindula dejone showed no response to 20E or EcR antagonist injections at the wandering stage.
source: Injections of 20E into female wanderers reared at low temperature (and with lower 20E titers) and of an EcR antagonist, CucB, into female wanderers reared at high temperature (and with higher 20E titers), showed no response across the first three species
evidence: This is supported by the injection experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Doleschallia bisaltide showed no response to 20E or EcR antagonist injections at the wandering stage.
source: Injections of 20E into female wanderers reared at low temperature (and with lower 20E titers) and of an EcR antagonist, CucB, into female wanderers reared at high temperature (and with higher 20E titers), showed no response across the first three species
evidence: This is supported by the injection experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eyespot size significantly increased with 20E injections in B. anynana.
source: whereas eyespot size significantly increased with 20E injections and decreased with antagonist injections in B. anynana (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the injection experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eyespot size significantly decreased with EcR antagonist injections in B. anynana.
source: whereas eyespot size significantly increased with 20E injections and decreased with antagonist injections in B. anynana (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the injection experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Only the eyespots of B. anynana are sensitive to 20E signaling at the wandering stage, within the natural range of titers displayed by these species.
source: These data indicate that only the eyespots of B. anynana are sensitive to 20E signaling at the wandering stage, within the natural range of titers displayed by these species.
evidence: This is inferred from the injection experiment data comparing responses across species.

claim: Eyespot sensitivity to 20E at the wandering stage is a derived trait potentially restricted to the satyrid sub-family within nymphalids.
source: This sensitivity is a derived trait potentially restricted to the satyrid sub-family within nymphalids (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative injection experiment data and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The evolution of plasticity in hormone titers, the evolution of hormone receptor expression in the trait, and the evolution of eyespot sensitivity to these hormones all took place at different stages of nymphalid diversification.
source: Our work showed that the evolution of plasticity in hormone titers, the evolution of hormone receptor expression in the trait, and the evolution of eyespot sensitivity to these hormones all took place at different stages of nymphalid diversification (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: An increase in eyespot size in response to temperature appears to be restricted to satyrid butterflies.
source: An increase in eyespot size in response to temperature appears to be restricted to satyrid butterflies, and is a derived response within nymphalids.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative rearing experiments and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: An increase in eyespot size in response to temperature is a derived response within nymphalids.
source: An increase in eyespot size in response to temperature appears to be restricted to satyrid butterflies, and is a derived response within nymphalids.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative rearing experiments and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Plasticity in eyespot size in butterflies had been primarily documented in satyrid butterflies such as Melanitis leda and several Bicyclus species.
source: Plasticity in eyespot size in butterflies had been primarily documented in satyrid butterflies such as Melanitis leda and several Bicyclus species (Brakefield, 1987; Roskam and Brakefield, 1999; van Bergen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In satyrid butterflies, eyespot size was always found to increase with rearing temperature.
source: Plasticity in eyespot size in butterflies had been primarily documented in satyrid butterflies such as Melanitis leda and several Bicyclus species (Brakefield, 1987; Roskam and Brakefield, 1999; van Bergen et al., 2017) where size was always found to increase with rearing temperature.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most of the reared species of nymphalids and the papilionid species showed a slight decrease in eyespot/spot size with an increase in temperature.
source: Most of the reared species of nymphalids and the papilionid species showed a slight decrease in eyespot/spot size with an increase in temperature, while some species showed no plasticity at all.
evidence: This is supported by the rearing experiment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some species showed no plasticity in eyespot/spot size at all.
source: Most of the reared species of nymphalids and the papilionid species showed a slight decrease in eyespot/spot size with an increase in temperature, while some species showed no plasticity at all.
evidence: This is supported by the rearing experiment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The decrease in eyespot size with increasing temperature may simply reflect non-adaptive variation from a poorly canalized system.
source: This decrease in eyespot size with increasing temperature may simply reflect non-adaptive variation from a poorly canalized system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Satyrid butterflies used the 20E asymmetry to regulate the size of their eyespots in a novel way.
source: In addition, satyrid butterflies, but none of the other species, used the 20E asymmetry to regulate the size of their eyespots in a novel way.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative hormone manipulation experiments.

claim: The recruitment of EcR to the eyespot central cells was enabled prior to the novel use of 20E asymmetry, perhaps concurrently with eyespot origins.
source: This was enabled by the prior recruitment of EcR to the eyespot central cells perhaps concurrently with eyespot origins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Central signaling cells play an important role in determining eyespot size at the wandering stages of development.
source: These central signaling cells play an important role in determining eyespot size at the wandering stages of development (Monteiro et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Some species, such as Junonia coenia, retain expression of EcR in eyespots but only at other stages of wing development.
source: Some species, such as Junonia coenia, retain expression of EcR in eyespots but only at other stages of wing development (Koch et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The active 20E-EcR complexes increase eyespot size in B. anynana but not in other species with similar EcR expression in their eyespot centers.
source: Finally, the active 20E-EcR complexes increase eyespot size in B. anynana but not in other species with similar EcR expression in their eyespot centers.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative hormone manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ability of 20E to promote localized patterns of cell division might have evolved in the lineage leading to B. anynana alone.
source: The ability of 20E to promote localized patterns of cell division might have evolved in the lineage leading to B. anynana alone (Bhardwaj et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the comparative data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Eyespot size plasticity in connection with wet and dry seasonal forms is widely conserved across the sub-family Nymphalinae.
source: Eyespot size plasticity in connection with wet and dry seasonal forms is widely conserved across the sub-family Nymphalinae (Clarke, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Different mechanisms may have evolved to regulate eyespot size plasticity in nymphalinae lineages compared to B. anynana.
source: Eyespot size plasticity in connection with wet and dry seasonal forms is widely conserved across the sub-family Nymphalinae (Clarke, 2017) but our results suggest that different mechanisms may have evolved to regulate eyespot size plasticity in these lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative experimental results showing different responses to temperature and hormone manipulation.

claim: All nymphalinae species tested (Vanessa cardui, Junonia almana, J. coenia, J. atlites, J. iphita and Doleschallia bisaltide) produced only small changes in the size of their Cu1 eyespots in response to rearing temperature.
source: Our controlled rearing experiments showed that all nymphalinae (Vanessa cardui, Junonia almana, J. coenia, J. atlites, J. iphita and Doleschallia bisaltide) produced only small changes in the size of the their Cu1 eyespots in response to rearing temperature, and these were in the opposite direction to those observed in B. anynana.
evidence: This is supported by the rearing experiment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The changes in Cu1 eyespot size in nymphalinae species were in the opposite direction to those observed in B. anynana.
source: Our controlled rearing experiments showed that all nymphalinae (Vanessa cardui, Junonia almana, J. coenia, J. atlites, J. iphita and Doleschallia bisaltide) produced only small changes in the size of the their Cu1 eyespots in response to rearing temperature, and these were in the opposite direction to those observed in B. anynana.
evidence: This is supported by the rearing experiment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Other environmental factors might cue and regulate seasonal morphs in nymphalinae species.
source: Other environmental factors might cue and regulate these species' seasonal morphs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), perhaps cues that better predict the arrival of the seasons where these butterflies have evolved.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation that temperature alone does not produce the expected seasonal forms.

claim: Phenotypic plasticity in ventral (Cu1) eyespot size in B. anynana hindwings is a complex, step-wise adaptation to seasonal environments cued by temperature that required very specific mutations to evolve.
source: For now, we uncover phenotypic plasticity in ventral (Cu1) eyespot size in B. anynana hindwings as a complex, step-wise adaptation to seasonal environments cued by temperature that required very specific mutations to evolve.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the comparative phylogenetic and experimental analysis.

claim: If many forms of adaptive plasticity are as specific and hard to evolve as the one documented in B. anynana, these exquisite adaptations to specific predictable fluctuating environments may lend the species vulnerable to extinction under unpredictable climate change.
source: This work also serves as a warning that if many forms of adaptive plasticity are as specific and hard to evolve as the one documented in B. anynana, these exquisite adaptations to specific predictable fluctuating environments may in fact, lend the species vulnerable to extinction under unpredictable climate change, as previously noted (Oostra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the findings, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the hot wet season, large exposed ventral eyespots in Bicyclus species help deflect attacks of invertebrate predators, or naïve vertebrate predators towards the wing margins.
source: In the hot wet season, the large exposed ventral eyespots help deflect attacks of invertebrate predators, or naïve vertebrate predators towards the wing margins (Lyytinen et al., 2004; Olofsson et al., 2010; Prudic et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on eyespot function.

claim: In the cool dry season, smaller eyespots in Bicyclus species help in camouflage against vertebrate predation.
source: whereas in the cool dry season the smaller eyespots help in camouflage against vertebrate predation (Lyytinen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on eyespot function.

claim: Bicyclus species live throughout dry and wet seasons in Africa.
source: Bicyclus species live throughout dry and wet seasons in Africa, where eyespots of different sizes serve different ecological roles (Brakefield and Reitsma, 1991; Brakefield et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ecological studies.

claim: Eyespots of different sizes serve different ecological roles in Bicyclus species.
source: Bicyclus species live throughout dry and wet seasons in Africa, where eyespots of different sizes serve different ecological roles (Brakefield and Reitsma, 1991; Brakefield et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ecological studies.

claim: Twelve species from different nymphalid sub-families and from tropical or sub-tropical regions, plus one outgroup papilionid species were reared at two different temperatures separated by 10°C.
source: To test these hypotheses and to examine how plasticity in B. anynana evolved, we reared twelve species from different nymphalid sub-families, and from tropical, or sub-tropical regions, plus one outgroup papilionid species (Figure 1—source data 1—Table S1) at two different temperatures, separated by 10°C, and measured spot and eyespot size plasticity in adult females.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Three different types of reaction norm to rearing temperature were observed across species.
source: Three different types of reaction norm to rearing temperature were observed across species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The wandering stage is the critical period for regulation of Cu1 eyespot size plasticity in ventral hindwings of B. anynana.
source: To investigate the molecular basis for how these distinct patterns of plasticity differed from that of B. anynana we compared 20E titers and EcR expression across species using female data, and focused exclusively on examining data for the critical period of development that was previously discovered for the regulation of Cu1 eyespot size plasticity in ventral hindwings of B. anynana, for example the wandering stage of larval development.
evidence: This is stated as previously discovered knowledge about B. anynana development.

claim: Mapping origins of eyespot size plasticity via maximum parsimony phylogenetic analysis suggests three independent origins for two different patterns of plasticity in the lineage with eyespots.
source: Mapping origins of eyespot size plasticity via maximum parsimony phylogenetic analysis suggests three independent origins for two different patterns of plasticity in the lineage with eyespots (eyespot size decreases with increasing temperatures: red lineages, and eyespot size increases with increasing temperature: blue lineage).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lineage leading to Satyrid butterflies gained a positive response to plasticity.
source: The lineage leading to Satyrid butterflies gained a positive response to plasticity (blue arrowhead), whereas most other Nymphalids had either no response, or limited negative plasticity response (red arrowhead).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most other Nymphalids had either no response, or limited negative plasticity response.
source: The lineage leading to Satyrid butterflies gained a positive response to plasticity (blue arrowhead), whereas most other Nymphalids had either no response, or limited negative plasticity response (red arrowhead).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 20E titer plasticity in response to temperature is an ancestral trait shared across butterflies, with a likely origin before the origin of eyespots.
source: 20E titers increase with an increase in rearing temperature across most species. This trait is ancestral in nature, with a likely origin before the origin of eyespots.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis of 20E titer data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EcR is absent in simple spots.
source: EcR is absent in simple spots, but present in the future eyespot centers of most of the species investigated (N ≥ 3 for each immunostaining: numbers in superscript represent sample size; Scale bars,10µm).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EcR is present in the future eyespot centers of most of the species investigated.
source: EcR is absent in simple spots, but present in the future eyespot centers of most of the species investigated (N ≥ 3 for each immunostaining: numbers in superscript represent sample size; Scale bars,10µm).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis suggests three independent origins for two different patterns of eyespot size plasticity (eyespot size decreases with increasing temperatures and eyespot size increases with increasing temperature).
source: Phylogenetic analysis suggests three independent origins for two different patterns of eyespot size plasticity (eyespot size decreases with increasing temperatures: red lineages and red circles, and eyespot size increases with increasing temperature: blue lineage and blue circles).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: EcR expression in eyespots is inferred to have originated concurrently with the origin of eyespots, about 85 Mya.
source: EcR expression in eyespots is inferred to have originated concurrently with the origin of eyespots, about 85 Mya, and subsequently lost in a few nymphalid lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: EcR expression in eyespots was subsequently lost in a few nymphalid lineages.
source: EcR expression in eyespots is inferred to have originated concurrently with the origin of eyespots, about 85 Mya, and subsequently lost in a few nymphalid lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.
